The green compacts are uniaxially pressed to 50-60% of theoretical density and may be cold isostatically pressed.
The ceramic workpieces are placed in an open or closed crucible and are directly exposed to the 83 GHz millimeter-wave beam.
The beam is focused to an elliptical shape of approximately 1 cm by 4 cm, which is adequate for processing small compacts.
The absorbed power per unit volume in a ceramic is proportional to the microwave frequency and the dielectric loss of the material.
Oxide ceramics tend to be more absorbing at higher temperatures and higher frequencies.
The beam power is a few kilowatts and the intensity is a few 100 W/cm2 at sintering temperatures.
The vacuum chamber operates at a pressure between 25 and 100 milliTorr.
Temperature is monitored using an S-type thermocouple and a remote two-color pyrometer.
YAG and yttria have been sintered with the millimeter-wave beam to up to 99% theoretical density.
Factors that impact the quality of the sintered materials include agglomerates, impurities, processing atmosphere, sintering aids, and thermal gradients.
Millimeter-wave sintering can result in superior microstructure with fewer trapped pores, cleaner grain boundaries, and smaller grain size compared to conventional sintering.
The resistive heater is used for pre-sintering heat treatments of the ceramic workpieces.
The quasi-optical beam system is used for focusing and manipulating the millimeter-wave beam.
The gyrotron-based material processing facility at NRL can generate between 1 W/cm2 and 2 kW/cm2 irradiance.
The millimeter-wave beam furnace is located inside a large processing chamber to confine the radiation.
